In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we prefer the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
h(x)={\int }_{x}^{2\pi }\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{2\pi }^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{x}^{2\pi }\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{2\pi }^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{2\pi }^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${h}^{′}(\pi ),$ we substitute $x=\pi $ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
